stamp: Okiru ESG Intelligence Toolkit  ·  Open methodology questions  ·  v1.0  ·  10 September 2026

sections.title: The numbers we grade against
sections.blurb: Each of these is a pass mark the toolkit applies today that nobody outside this office has approved. Where a target should differ by sector or company size, please say so — that is the part we cannot guess.

questions.question: Which of our targets hold for any South African company, and which must change by sector or size?
questions.context: we grade every company against the same eight: 10% annual emissions reduction, 20% renewable electricity, 75% waste diverted from landfill, 60% Black employees, 16 training hours per employee, injury rate of 2.0, 1% of profit on community spend, 40% local procurement.

questions.question: Should a lost-time injury frequency rate be expressed per 200 000 or per 1 000 000 hours worked, and what rate marks genuinely good performance?
questions.context: we use 2.0 per 200 000 hours as the pass mark, for every industry.

questions.question: For a 60% Black representation target, is the percentage taken over the whole workforce, or over management only?
questions.context: we take it over the whole workforce, at all occupational levels.

questions.question: For a 30% Black-women-in-management target, which occupational levels count as management?
questions.context: we count the top three occupational levels.

questions.question: Should 80% mandatory grant recovery be measured against the full 1% skills development levy the company paid, or only against the portion it can actually claim back?
questions.context: we measure it against the full levy.

sections.title: What stops us publishing a defensible figure
sections.blurb: These are the ones that block us outright: without them we cannot put an emissions number or a tax estimate in front of a bank, a customer or SARS and defend it.

questions.question: Which published emission-factor set — name, edition year and table — should we cite for diesel, petrol, LPG, grid electricity, on-site solar, municipal water and landfilled waste? For grid electricity specifically, what factor applies to a year ending in 2025 or 2026?
questions.context: the factors are in the system but not one carries a source or a version, so no emissions figure can be traced back to anything. Our grid figure is 0,82 kg CO₂e per kWh, origin unknown.

questions.question: Where a company generates and consumes its own solar power, should reported Scope 2 simply be the electricity bought from the grid, with the solar shown separately as renewable share or avoided emissions?
questions.context: we subtract solar as a negative line inside the emissions inventory itself.

questions.question: Under the Carbon Tax Act, is a company taxed only on the fuel it burns itself, or do the emissions from grid electricity it buys also form part of its taxable total?
questions.context: we tax direct and purchased-electricity emissions together.

questions.question: What minimum set of questions establishes whether a company is liable for carbon tax at all — and can a retailer, law firm or school that only buys electricity and runs a few vehicles ever be liable?
questions.context: we produce a tax estimate for every company, with no liability test at all.

questions.question: For a 2025/26 reporting year, which rand-per-tonne carbon tax rate applies — and what exactly is the R640 rate?
questions.context: we hold two rates, R236 and R640, without knowing which applies to which year or which emissions.

questions.question: Which value-chain emission categories must a report include before a bank, a listed customer or a tender reviewer accepts it as complete, and in what order should we add them?
questions.context: we capture one category — municipal water — out of fifteen, and label the total "partial".

questions.question: Which one or two intensity ratios should a South African company report alongside absolute tonnes, and which do lenders and tender evaluators here actually expect to see?
questions.context: we report absolute tonnes only. No intensity denominator — per rand, per tonne-kilometre, per employee — exists anywhere in the system.

sections.title: What counts as proof, and what to do with a blank
sections.blurb: Each of these decides whether a company gets full marks, no marks, or is left out of the scoring entirely. Getting them wrong quietly moves a score by several points.

questions.question: For the governance questions answered Yes, Partial or No — Social and Ethics Committee, code of ethics and hotline, POPIA Information Officer, climate risk on the board agenda, ESG-linked executive pay — what single document would an assurance provider accept as proof for each, and what shortfall makes an answer Partial rather than Yes?
questions.context: the company self-rates each one and we award points on the rating alone. No evidence is requested or tested.

questions.question: A company that had no health-and-safety incidents at all during the year: full marks, no marks, or excluded with its weighting moved elsewhere?
questions.context: it scores zero — the same as a company that had incidents and investigated none of them.

questions.question: When a company marks a climate-disclosure requirement as not applicable to its business, should it be excluded from the readiness percentage, counted as not met, or counted as met?
questions.context: we count it as not met, which marks the company down for a requirement that does not apply to it.

questions.question: When an indicator cannot apply to a company at all — a food-safety supplier rating for a business with no food in its supply chain — should those points come out of its total, or be scored as zero?
questions.context: they score zero, so the company is marked down for something it could never have had.

questions.question: What makes a regulatory penalty "material" — a rand threshold, a share of revenue or profit? Which regulators are in scope, and over what period?
questions.context: the company decides for itself what counts as material, and we score its answer.

sections.title: Where the workbook only fits a distributor
sections.blurb: The workbook was built around a road-freight FMCG distributor. These four decide what a bank, a mine, a school or a manufacturer does instead — we would rather code a rule than hardcode a client.

questions.question: For a bank, a hospital and a school, how should the environmental, social and governance pillars be weighted against one another?
questions.context: all fourteen sectors inherit one FMCG distributor's weighting and thresholds unchanged.

questions.question: Must energy, water, fuel and waste be broken down by individual operating site, or is a company-wide total acceptable? If a site breakdown is expected, what counts as a site?
questions.context: the workbook has five fixed depot rows and nine fixed months. A company with one site, or fifty, has nowhere correct to put its data.

questions.question: Must a company decide and state for itself which entities its emissions cover — everything it operates, everything it financially controls, or only its ownership share of each business it part-owns?
questions.context: we state "operational control" on every report without ever asking the client.

questions.question: Should every company follow the same fixed schedule of cuts — 5% by 2026, 20% by 2028, 50% by 2030, 90% by 2045 — or must the annual rate be worked out from each company's own baseline year and target year?
questions.context: one fixed calendar schedule is applied to every company, so a firm with a 2019 baseline gets no credit for cuts already made.
